speaker: Nima Arkani-Hamed
title: In Conversation with Nima Arkani-Hamed
question: In theoretical physics, what is the main structural obstacle preventing spacetime-free geometric formulations of particle scattering from covering all forces of nature?
guest: In scattering of elementary particles, the actual question is not posed on the inside of a region of spacetime with particle trajectories interacting. It's just a question about a bunch of momentum vectors coming in and going out. That's the canvas in which we're trying to build an alternate mathematical picture. It seems like an empty and austere world, yet with very few assumptions something magical happens. One of the most important elements allowing this in the mathematics is imagining these vectors aren't handed to you randomly, but in a particular order: particle one, two, three, four, and so on. That innocuous thing turns out in physics to be closely related to particles having color, as in the strong and weak interactions, where the way colors flow from one particle to the next is responsible for this ordering. All our progress has centered on particles with color. Yet some of the most important things—photons and gravity—have no notion of color or ordering. Because ordering seemed like the lifeline that let something happen out of seemingly nothing, understanding what organizing principle replaces it without color is the largest open problem.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main obstacle is that these formulations, most famously the amplituhedron, depend on special structure that only highly symmetric, idealized theories possess, and gravity and real-world forces lack it.

The amplituhedron works for planar N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. In the planar (large number of colours) limit, particles have a fixed cyclic ordering. That ordering allows a single, well-defined loop integrand, a hidden dual conformal (Yangian) symmetry, and the "positivity" conditions that define the geometric object, whose volume-like canonical form gives the amplitude.

Gravity has no colour ordering: gravitons carry no colour labels, so there is no planar limit, no canonical ordering of external particles, and no unique loop integrand. The positive-Grassmannian structure therefore has nothing obvious to attach to. Gravity amplitudes also have worse high-energy behaviour, and their poles are not organised in the same simple way.

Similar problems arise for non-planar and non-supersymmetric theories such as real QCD. Partial progress exists, including associahedra and "surfaceology" for simpler coloured scalar theories, and hints of positivity in gravity, but no complete positive geometry for gravity is known.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: The main structural obstacle is the absence of color ordering in colorless, intrinsically non-planar interactions, above all gravity. Existing spacetime-free formulations, including positive geometries like the amplituhedron and associahedron as well as curve-integral ("surfaceology") methods, rely on non-Abelian color structure to decompose scattering into partial amplitudes with a fixed cyclic ordering of external particles along the boundaries of auxiliary surfaces. Even where surfaceology extends gauge and matter theories beyond supersymmetry and planarity to higher-genus surfaces, this cyclic ordering still provides canonical global kinematic and loop variables that map physical factorization channels onto geometric boundaries. Gravitons, however, carry no color charge: gravitational amplitudes must be fully permutation-invariant across all external particles, leaving no canonical way to assign global planar or surface variables across non-planar topologies. Compounding this, gravity exhibits non-logarithmic singularities, such as higher-order poles at infinity, which violate the purely logarithmic ($d\log$) boundary axioms of positive geometry.

noweb.answer:
The central structural obstacle is that spacetime-free positive geometries—such as the amplituhedron, kinematic associahedra, and surfaceology—rely fundamentally on planar cyclic ordering and purely logarithmic singularities, both of which break down for gravity and realistic chiral matter.

In gauge theories like Yang–Mills, color charges organize interactions into cyclically ordered, planar diagrams on bordered surfaces, allowing polytopes or curve combinatorics to encode scattering channels. Gravitons, however, carry no color charge: gravitational scattering is intrinsically non-planar and invariant under all particle permutations, leaving no boundary ordering to anchor an auxiliary surface or polytope. Furthermore, positive geometries are defined by canonical differential forms with strictly logarithmic ($d\log$) singularities, whereas gravity’s spin-2 derivative couplings generate higher-order, non-logarithmic poles at kinematic infinity, and multi-loop amplitudes introduce elliptic and higher-genus structures beyond standard polylogarithmic forms. Even outside gravity, extending these frameworks to the full Standard Model remains obstructed because chiral electroweak interactions and fermion chirality break the real positivity and bosonic combinatorics on which known geometric formulations depend.

models.answer:
The main obstacle is that these geometric formulations depend on planarity, meaning a fixed cyclic ordering of particles. Examples include the amplituhedron, the associahedron, and the newer "surfaceology" or curve-integral program.

That ordering comes from colour (gauge-group) structure in the large‑N limit. It is what supplies the "dual" momentum coordinates and the positivity conditions that define a polytope-like region whose canonical form gives the amplitude. Gauge theories with colour, especially planar N=4 super‑Yang–Mills and colour-ordered scalar theories, fit this framework well.

Gravity has no colour, so its amplitudes are fully permutation-symmetric and intrinsically non-planar. Without an ordering there is no natural kinematic space and no positivity structure from which a geometry could be built. Beyond leading order in large N, the non-planar parts of gauge theories have the same problem, because the integrands lack global loop variables and a well-defined positive region.

There are secondary problems too: the strongest results rely on maximal supersymmetry, and realistic chiral matter with massive particles is hard to include. The core barrier, though, is extending these geometries beyond planar, colour-ordered theories, above all to gravity.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: The main structural obstacle is the reliance of spacetime-free geometric frameworks—such as the amplituhedron, associahedron, and surfaceology—on a fixed cyclic ordering of external particles. In colored gauge theories like Yang–Mills, non-Abelian color charges naturally supply this ordering in the planar limit, which defines the positivity conditions, boundaries, and canonical forms from which locality and unitarity emerge. However, gravity and Abelian forces like electromagnetism have no color charge and therefore no intrinsic ordering: graviton and photon amplitudes are completely symmetric under permutations of external particles. Without an inherent ordering, standard notions of total positivity, planar kinematic variables, and a single well-defined loop integrand break down, leaving non-planar loop corrections and gravity without an analogous positive geometry. Although color–kinematics duality links gravity amplitudes to gauge theories through the double copy, constructing an intrinsically permutation-symmetric, ordering-free geometry—while also accommodating realistic Standard Model features such as massive particles, chiral matter, and non-supersymmetric dynamics—remains an unsolved challenge.

noweb.answer: The main structural obstacle is that existing spacetime-free geometric frameworks—such as the amplituhedron and the associahedron—rely heavily on a fixed cyclic ordering of external particles, a structure that arises naturally only in the planar limit of color-ordered gauge theories. In realistic theories of nature, this ordering breaks down: non-planar corrections in Yang-Mills theory mix color structures, and gravity has no color ordering at all because gravitons are completely permutation-symmetric. Without a canonical ordering to define the boundaries and facets of a positive geometry, it is far harder to construct a single geometric object whose canonical differential form reproduces the full scattering amplitude and its physical singularities. Compounding this geometric hurdle, current formulations work best for idealized, massless, and often maximally supersymmetric models. Extending them to the full Standard Model and quantum gravity also requires accommodating massive particles, broken symmetries, ultraviolet divergences, and running couplings, all of which complicate the clean pole structure that positive geometries encode.
